Classifying Life: The Leopard

Text description of this image

The leopard is classified in a nested hierarchy that narrows from broad to specific: domain Eukarya, kingdom Animalia, phylum Chordata, class Mammalia, order Carnivora, family Felidae, genus Panthera, and species Panthera pardus. Each level sits inside the one before it, and the other two domains, Bacteria and Archaea, are shown for comparison.

The Idea of Fixed Species

  • Stunning discoveries in the early 1800s, including fossilized skeletons of a gigantic sea creature dubbed an ichthyosaur, or fish-lizard, convinced many naturalists that extinctions had indeed occurred.

Explaining the Diversity of Life

  • The explanation of the origin of the diversity of life accepted by present-day biologists is the evolutionary theory, proposed by Charles Darwin in his best-known book, On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, published in 1859.
Text description of this image

The text reads: “By Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life. By Charles Darwin, M.A. … London: John Murray, Albemarle Street. 1859.”

Text description of this image

The timeline places Darwin’s work in the context of earlier ideas. Hutton’s gradualism (1795), Malthus’s essay on population (1798), Lamarck’s hypothesis of evolution (1809), Cuvier’s fossil studies (1812), and Lyell’s Principles of Geology (1830) preceded Darwin’s voyage around the world on HMS Beagle (1831–1836). Darwin wrote his essay on descent with modification in 1844. In 1858 Wallace, studying species in the Malay Archipelago, sent Darwin his own hypothesis of natural selection, and On the Origin of Species was published in 1859. A photo of the Galápagos Islands accompanies the timeline.

Text description of this image

A red line traces the route of Darwin’s voyage around the world, passing South America, the Galápagos Islands, New Zealand, Australia, and the Cape of Good Hope.

Anatomical Homology

Text description of this image

The same set of bones, the humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals, and phalanges, appears in the forelimbs of a human, cat, whale, and bat. The color coding shows that each bone matches across the four limbs even though shape and proportion differ with how the animal uses its limb.

Evolution: Darwin’s Theory

  • There are many lines of evidence for Darwin’s theory of evolution, the idea that living species
    are descendants of ancestral species that were different from present-day ones.
Text description of this image

Four animals are shown from top to bottom: Pakicetus, Rodhocetus, Dorudon, and living cetaceans. Next to each is a drawing of its hind-limb bones, color-coded in the key as pelvis, femur, tibia, and foot. The limb is complete in Pakicetus, shrinks to a small cluster of bones in Dorudon, and in living cetaceans only a small pelvis bone remains.

Text description of this image

From the base, the branches lead in order to lungfishes, amphibians, mammals, lizards and snakes, crocodiles, ostriches, and hawks and other birds. Tetrapod limbs are marked at the branch leading to amphibians and all later groups, the amnion at the branch leading to mammals and all later groups, and feathers at the branch leading to birds. Brackets at the right group tetrapods (amphibians through birds), amniotes (mammals through birds), and birds.

Genetic Drift

  • Genetic Drift
Text description of this image

Generation 1: p = 0.7, q = 0.3. Only 5 of 10 plants leave offspring. Generation 2: p = 0.5, q = 0.5. Only 2 of 10 plants leave offspring. Generation 3: p = 1.0, q = 0.0, and every plant is red, so the white allele is lost.

Gene Flow

  • Gene flow
    • is another source of evolutionary change,
    • is genetic exchange with another population,
    • may result in the gain or loss of alleles, and
    • tends to reduce genetic differences between populations.
Text description of this image

At the top, the original population shows a bell-shaped distribution of fur color. (a) Directional selection favors one extreme, so the distribution shifts toward it. (b) Disruptive selection favors both extremes, so the distribution splits into two peaks. (c) Stabilizing selection favors the middle, so the distribution narrows.
